query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Partial ordering induced by short-duration, moderate-temperature annealing in as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy alloy thin films broadens the first-order magnetostructural transition and lowers hysteresis by refining microstructure and reducing lattice strain heterogeneities, thereby governing the magnetocaloric response under low magnetic fields.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi thin films formed by magnetron co-sputtering, exhibiting a disordered microstructure and a sharp, hysteretic magnetostructural transition
generation.intervention: A brief thermal annealing step (e.g., 300–500 °C for short durations) to promote partial ordering and microstructural refinement while avoiding full phase transformation
generation.conditions: Controlled sputter power and substrate temperature during deposition; optimized time–temperature annealing profile after deposition
generation.structural_mediator: Transition from a predominantly disordered state toward partially ordered crystalline domains, reducing intrinsic strain and compositional inhomogeneities
generation.mechanism: Local partial ordering and refined domain structure decrease the abruptness of the magnetostructural transition, extending the temperature range of the magnetocaloric effect and diminishing hysteresis losses by moderating sudden lattice distortions and exchange energy distributions
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited baseline, annealed films show a broader but slightly reduced peak in isothermal entropy change, with a significant (e.g., up to ~20–40%) reduction in hysteresis and improved reversibility under low applied fields
generation.baseline: Unannealed, as-deposited films with a sharp, sizable magnetocaloric peak but excessive hysteresis that undermines efficiency
generation.boundary: Behavior holds for moderate annealing times and temperatures up to ~500 °C in FeMnNiGeSi films of similar composition; excessive annealing or high temperatures causing grain coarsening could negate these benefits
generation.uncertainty: Precise magnitudes and optimal annealing regimes are not definitively established due to limited published data on FeMnNiGeSi films; further experiments are required to quantify the exact hysteresis reduction and MCE broadening

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of thin-film samples by magnetron co-sputtering: one kept as-deposited and one subjected to short annealing at ~300–500 °C. Characterize microstructures and measure magnetization and magnetocaloric properties under ~1–2 T fields near the transition temperature.
measurements: XRD and TEM to reveal grain size, ordering state, and domain characteristics
Magnetization loops for hysteresis quantification in the temperature region of the magnetostructural transition
Isothermal entropy change and magnetocaloric effect curves to determine broadening and amplitude changes
Microstructural stability under repeated thermal cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If annealed samples do not exhibit a significant broadening of the magnetocaloric transition or a measurable decrease in hysteresis relative to the as-deposited control, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Delving deeper, unfortunately, RCP tends to overestimate the merits of the materials which have a large temperature range of magnetocaloric effect (δTFWHM) but small entropy changes [,] in no small part because materials with same relative cooling power can behave differently in a magnetic cooling simulation []. Moreover, one of the last printed books about magnetic cooling ignores this figure of merit []. In order to be of use in magnetic refrigeration applications the chosen materials have to show a large magnetocaloric effect—a large magnetic entropy change. Besides this, there is a list of requirements related with heat transfer, heat capacity, heat conductivity, chemical and mechanical stability, hysteresis losses, eddy currents losses, etc. Therefore, magnetic measurements can be a trusted guide in deciding if a material deserves the effort of complete characterization. Some compounds of the type A1−xBxMnO3 can be considered to be of interest for magnetic refrigeration because some of these compounds show −ΔSm values (−ΔSm ≈ 4–6 J·kg−1·K−1 for ΔH = 5 T) comparable to intermetallic alloys []. This is the case of our investigated compounds.

In summary, we demonstrate a low-cost, low-temperature, and scalable synthesis approach of single-phase spinel magnetic HEO NPs including up to eight metal elements by utilizing electrospun and post-electrospun ambient annealing processes. The metal nitrate precursors were enveloped in cellulose acetate nanofibers during electrospinning. The homogenous HEO NPs could be generated by annealing the nanofibers at 330 °C for 30 minutes. The 8-HEO (Fe–Co–Ni–Cr–Cu–Mg–Zn–Mn) NPs possess a diameter of 33.7 nm and the spinel single-phase structure was confirmed with the uniform elemental distribution. The XPS spectrum of each element proves the oxidation state of HEO NPs and demonstrates the multivalent of the magnetic elements in the spinel structure. This electrospinning method possesses several advantages including the low-temperature synthesis of HEOs, uniform premixture in the precursors of the metal ions, flexibility to tune the elements in HEOs, and low cost of the HEO nanoparticles for upscale manufacturing. The unpredictability of geopolitical tensions and resulting supply chain and pricing instabilities make it imperative to explore rare earth free magnetic materials. As such, we have investigated fully transition metal based “high entropy alloys” in the context of the magnetocaloric effect. We find the NiFeCoCrPdx family exhibits a second order magnetic phase transition whose critical temperature is tunable from 100 K to well above room temperature. The system notably displays changes in the functionality of the magnetic entropy change depending on x, which leads to nearly 40% enhancement of the refrigerant capacity. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior provides direct evidence that heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy. The general implications of this work are that the parent NiFeCoCr compound can be tuned dramatically with FCC metal additives. chosen.technique: magnetron co-sputtering with subsequent short-duration annealing
chosen.conditions: controlled sputter power, deposition temperature, and brief thermal treatment to refine microstructure
chosen.why: Creating thin or structured films directly addresses the limited heat-exchange rates by increasing surface-to-volume ratio, while a mild post-deposition annealing can mitigate the abrupt first-order transition to reduce hysteresis. This combination provides a clear test of the hypothesis that the as-deposited microstructure and partial ordering govern the magnetocaloric response under low-applied-field cycles.
